title: India's import duties are nearly 3 times China's and Vietnam's, says a report
subtitle: A Delhi think tank says costly parts and machines push up factory costs in India, and asks for fewer and lower duty rates.
content_html:
India taxes goods coming into the country almost three times as much as China and Vietnam do. That is the main finding of a report released on Wednesday, 18 November 2026 by the Foundation for Economic Development (FED), a think tank based in Delhi. The report says the average import duty India charges on non-farm goods is 10.8%. China's average is 3.7% and Vietnam's average is 3.5%.

The report says this raises costs for Indian factories and holds back the growth in goods India sells abroad. The UNI news agency also reported the same numbers on the same day.

What is an import duty?

An import duty is a tax a country charges when goods come in from abroad. Think of a toll gate at the edge of a city. Every truck pays a fee to enter. A bigger fee makes everything inside the truck cost more by the time it reaches the shop.

The duty does not only fall on finished goods like a ready phone or a car. India also taxes the raw materials, parts and machines that Indian factories bring in.

Why a tax on imports can hurt sellers abroad

Many Indian factories do not make every part themselves. They buy some parts and machines from other countries. The FED report says India taxes these inputs more heavily than rival countries do. India's average duty on factory inputs is 6.8%. That is twice China's 3.3% and nearly four times Vietnam's 1.8%.

Picture two samosa stalls on the same street. If one stall pays more for oil and flour, each samosa costs more to make. The other stall, with cheaper oil, can sell at a lower price and win the customer. Factories work the same way. A tax on a part quietly becomes part of the price of the final product.

Rahul Ahluwalia, founder and managing partner of FED, said this, as reported by The Economic Times:

"Every tariff on an input is an added cost and barrier for an Indian factory trying to sell to the world."

How big is the cost gap?

The report looks at three big groups of goods: electronics, engineering goods and apparel. Together, they make up $10.5 trillion of world trade. In these three, Indian goods cost 5 to 15% more to make than goods made in China and Vietnam. The report says input costs alone explain 60 to 77% of that gap.

There is one more number that shows the gap. Only about a quarter of India's imports come in at a duty of 2.5% or less. In China, 79% of imports come in at that low level. In Vietnam, it is 81%.

The problem of 44 different rates

High duties are one part of the story. The other part is how complicated the system is. India's tariff system has 44 different effective rates, the report says. This leads to disputes, delays and uncertainty for importers.

Imagine a college canteen with 44 different prices for the same cup of tea, depending on the cup, the sugar and the time of day. The cashier and the students would argue all day, and the queue would never move.

Another trade think tank, the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), has pointed to a related problem known as an inverted duty structure. This is when parts are taxed at a higher rate than the finished product made from them. GTRI says this hurts makers at home.

What does the FED report ask for?

The report wants lower and simpler duties, brought in step by step. It suggests moving, over time, to just three rates: 0%, 5% and 7.5%, including cess. A cess is an extra charge added on top of the duty. The report also wants more than 60% of imports to come in duty free.

The phone story the report points to

The report gives one example where lower duties helped. India cut import duties across the mobile phone chain, from parts to the finished handset. Over the same years, phone exports grew nearly seven times, from $4.4 billion in 2022 to $29.4 billion in 2026. The report says the number of people working in the sector more than tripled in that time.

Why the numbers are really about work

The report links duties to work for young Indians. It says India needs to grow at over 8% a year and create 80 lakh new roles every year. Demand at home alone is not enough for that, the report says.

So factory goods sold abroad need to grow by more than 10% a year. That is nearly double today's rate of 5.4%. The report says this faster growth could add $1.8 trillion in extra sales abroad over ten years.

The report also says countries with low average tariffs sell 13 times more abroad per person than countries with high tariffs. And if India matched Vietnam's share of world trade in electronics, engineering goods and apparel, it could create about 53 lakh more direct roles.

What has the government already done?

The government has already cut some duties on inputs. In the Union Budget for 2026 to 2027, it took customs duty to zero on aircraft parts and repair inputs, and cut or removed duties on critical minerals that factories need. The head of India's customs board told Outlook Business the focus was on strategic sectors and manufacturing.

This Moneycontrol video explains the customs changes made in Budget 2026.

This Mint video looks at the duty changes across sectors in the same Budget.

What this means for you

For now, this is a think tank's report, not a government decision. The idea behind it is easy to follow. In the report's view, when parts and machines cost less to bring in, Indian factories can make goods for less, win more orders abroad and create more work at home.

For anyone planning a career in a factory, in trade or in a small export business, duties on parts are worth understanding. They shape the price an Indian maker can offer a buyer in another country, as the cost gap with China and Vietnam shows.
